title: The First Passenger
question: A farmer ferries a wolf, a goat, and a cabbage, taking one per trip. Wolves eat goats; goats eat cabbage. Which crosses the river first?
correctExplanation: The goat — the middle item, threatened by one side and threatening the other, must shuttle. Ends travel once; middles thrice.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is the goat. Only the middle item can wait safely on either bank at each stage: wolf-first strands goat-with-cabbage (eaten), cabbage-first strands wolf-with-goat (eaten). Pivots travel first and last.
lessonContent:
Middle items shuttle first and last.
Threatened-and-threatening defines pivots.
Ends travel once; middles thrice.
Identify pivots before loading boats.

title: The Seven Crossings
question: For the wolf-goat-cabbage trio with a one-item boat, every return trip except none is needed — the goat shuttles back twice. What is the minimum crossing count?
correctExplanation: 7 crossings: goat over, back empty... precisely goat, return, wolf, goat back, cabbage, return, goat. Two returns, seven legs.
incorrectExplanation: Close — the answer is 7. The goat crosses three times (over, back, over... plus final): two loaded returns are unavoidable with one incompatible pair at each stage. Count legs, not wishes.
lessonContent:
Legs counted beat wishes hoped.
Two returns are unavoidable here.
Shuttles triple middles routinely.
Minimums prove by exhaustion plus construction.

title: The Roomy Boat
question: Same trio, but the boat now holds the farmer plus two items. How many river crossings suffice at minimum?
correctExplanation: 3 crossings: two items over, farmer back alone, last item over. Capacity dissolves the classic constraint.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is 3. Room for two converts seven legs into three: pair over, solo return, single over. Capacity changes everything; classic answers expire with classic boats.
lessonContent:
Capacity changes everything structural.
Classic answers expire with classic boats.
Pair over, solo back, single over.
Room dissolves constraints directly.

title: The Eleven Crossings
question: Three missionaries and three cannibals share a two-person boat; cannibals may never outnumber missionaries on either bank. What is the minimum crossing count?
correctExplanation: 11 crossings — the classic solution shuttles majorities carefully across five loaded forwards and... precisely eleven legs with six forward trips. Ratios rule rivers.
incorrectExplanation: Close — the answer is 11. Track majorities every leg: two cannibals over, one back, two more over, one back, two missionaries over, mixed pair back, two missionaries over, one cannibal back, two cannibals over, one back, two cannibals over. Eleven legs, zero violations.
lessonContent:
Majorities rule every river leg.
Track ratios, not just headcounts.
Eleven legs thread six-and-six safely.
Constraints compound across banks.

title: The Solo Limit
question: Same missionaries and cannibals, same two-person boat. On the very first trip, at most how many missionaries may board together?
correctExplanation: One — two missionaries first leaves one missionary facing three cannibals behind. Openings constrain like endgames.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is one. Board two and the left bank holds 1M against 3C: violation at departure. First trips obey the same ratios as lasts.

title: The Triple Ferry
question: Same six travelers, but the boat now holds three. What is the new minimum crossing count?

incorrectExplanation: Close — the answer is 5. Bigger boats compress shuttles: 3C over, 1C back, 3M over, 1M back, M+C over — all banks legal throughout. Check each arrival, not just departures.

title: The Single Berth
question: Same six travelers, but the boat now holds only one person and needs no rower — it drifts back empty on its own. Can everyone get across?
correctExplanation: Impossible — single berths move one at a time with empty returns: net progress per round trip is zero, and any bank left unbalanced violates ratios. Shuttles without pairing strand everyone.
incorrectExplanation: Not quite — the answer is impossible. One-at-a-time with empty returns nets zero per cycle, and unbalanced banks violate constraints at every intermediate stage. Capacity one cannot thread ratio rules.
lessonContent:
Net-zero cycles strand all travelers.

title: The Seventeen Minutes
question: Four hikers (1, 2, 7, 10 minutes) share one torch, crossing a bridge at most two at a time at the slower walker's pace, with the torch ferried back. What is the minimum total time?
correctExplanation: 17 minutes: 1+2 over (2), 1 back (1), 7+10 over (10), 2 back (2), 1+2 over (2). The two slowest share one slow crossing.
incorrectExplanation: Close — the answer is 17. Pair the slowest together (one slow trip, not two), escorted by the fastest shuttling: 2+1+10+2+2. Fifteen wishes, seventeen minimum.
lessonContent:
Slowest pair shares one slow trip.
Fastest shuttles escort the crossing.
Add legs, never wishes, for totals.
Seventeen is optimal, not obvious.
